title: Tamannaah Bhatia Names the 'Gaze' Nobody in South Cinema Says Out Loud — and Refuses to Call Her Dance Numbers 'Item Songs'
excerpt: In a candid Forbes India sit-down, the Baahubali star draws a line between goddesses and 'item girls', and quietly dismantles the patriarchal lens she says still defines stardom down South.
body:
She wakes up wanting to feel glamorous. **Tamannaah Bhatia** told Forbes India that in so many words — "glamour is very innate… I wake up wanting to feel glamorous" — and somehow it lands less like a confession than a thesis statement. Twenty-one years and 85-plus films in, the woman who crossed every linguistic border Indian cinema has drawn is done apologising for the shimmer. What she is not done doing is naming the thing nobody at a South Indian film party says into a microphone.

The headline she handed everyone was three words long: *patriarchal gaze*. Reflecting on her early days in Tollywood and Kollywood, she didn't reach for euphemism. "When I entered the south industry, I understood why people might call it many names," she said. "It's a very specific gaze. It's a patriarchal sort of vibe or it's a gaze that's not very complimentary."

> "It's a very specific gaze. It's a patriarchal sort of vibe or it's a gaze that's not very complimentary." — Tamannaah Bhatia, to Forbes India


![Forbes India — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/5/59/Forbes-India.jpg)



> **""The south needed to have that star quality to be able to pull that off, so I personally feel like that cinema is as or more restrictive in that sense," she said, careful to flag it as her own truth."**



Coming from almost anyone else this would read as a grievance. Coming from the actress who anchored *Baahubali*, headlined *Stree 2*, and remains one of the highest-paid women across three industries, it reads as field notes from inside the machine. And she pressed further — arguing the South is, in her experience, *more* restrictive than Bollywood for a woman trying to do it all. "The south needed to have that star quality to be able to pull that off, so I personally feel like that cinema is as or more restrictive in that sense," she said, careful to flag it as her own truth. In Hindi cinema, she pointed out, an actor can choose the artistic lane or the commercial one — "and the ones who do both inevitably become superstars."

What makes the interview crackle is that she refuses to let glamour be the villain of her own story. This is where Tamannaah gets genuinely interesting. She will not call a great dance number an "item song." To her, the very phrase is the patriarchal gaze in miniature — a way of shrinking a woman's most-watched four minutes into something disposable.

> "You might not remember those movies, but you will always remember a 'Chammak Challo', 'Sheila Ki Jawani' or 'Kamli'… They look like goddesses, they move like goddesses. They are just beauty personified." — Tamannaah Bhatia


![South Indian — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Tirumala_090615.jpg/3840px-Tirumala_090615.jpg)


It's a sharp reframe, and an undeniable one. Name the film *Sheila Ki Jawani* is from without Googling it. Now hum the hook — you already are. **Kareena Kapoor Khan** and **Katrina Kaif**, she argues, didn't decorate those films; they outlived them. "It's a party number, it's a dance number. So for me, that's how I look at this space. I don't look at it like an item," she said. From the elderly uncles to the grandmoms to the kids, everyone's on the floor for these songs at every wedding from Hyderabad to Houston. (Her own pick-me-up after a brutal day, she confessed, is dancing to **Himesh Reshammiya**. Iconic, frankly.)

She's also honest about the craft hiding under the sparkle. For *Aaj Ki Raat* in *Stree 2* she built the number around the character of Shama rather than a generic vamp; for *Ghafoor* in **Aryan Khan's** *The Ba***ds of Bollywood* she imagined a woman at an after-party. "It's borderline comical because 'Ghafoor' did not have sexy steps, but it had a very glamorous vibe," she laughed. The point being: the woman on screen is making a thousand decisions the gaze never bothers to notice.

The timing is what gives the whole conversation teeth. Her remarks land just as the makers of **Peddi** — the **Ram Charan** mega-vehicle — faced a public backlash over how **Janhvi Kapoor** was framed in promotional material, prompting edits and a social-media apology from director **Buchi Babu Sana**. Tamannaah didn't have to name the controversy. She didn't need to. She'd already drawn the map.

For the diaspora, this is the kind of star talk that travels better than any trailer. Tamannaah's *Stree 2* and *Lust Stories 2* stream on **Amazon Prime Video** and **Netflix** respectively across the US, UK and Canada, and her next big swing — the Tollywood entry *Odela 2* — is on the diaspora radar. But the most quotable thing she's released this year isn't a song. It's a sentence about a gaze. And she said it with a smile that dared anyone to look away.
